summary: This standards-track RFC defines the GSS-API pseudo-random function for the Kerberos V mechanism. It is based on the Kerberos cryptographic framework PRF, and lets applications derive keys from an established Kerberos security context.

plainLanguage.summary: Once two programs have a shared secret, they sometimes need more secret keys. This gives a way to make new ones from the first.

questions: what is the kerberos gss-api prf
does the kerberos prf counter start at 0 or 1
subtitle: How to derive extra key material from a Kerberos GSS-API security context, with the PRF+ counter fixed.

tldr.problem: Applications that already have an established Kerberos V GSS-API security context sometimes need more keys for their own protocols, and RFC 4402 counted from 1 while many implementations counted from 0.
tldr.mechanism: The PRF is a PRF+ construction: the Kerberos V pseudo-random function applied to a 32-bit counter concatenated with the input, using a key chosen from the context, with the blocks joined and truncated to the length requested.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4402, which is reclassified as Historic, and matches what implementations actually do.

today: RFC 7802 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 4402, which it reclassifies as Historic. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7802 specifies the pseudo-random function (PRF) for the Kerberos V mechanism of the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API). It is the Kerberos counterpart of the generic GSS-API PRF extension in RFC 4401, and it is a PRF+ style construction. Applications use it to key their own protocols once a Kerberos V GSS-API security context has been established.

The document uses the RFC 2119 key words MUST, SHOULD and so on in their standard sense.
sections.plainLanguage: After two programs have shared a secret, this gives them a fair way to make more keys from it.

sections.title: Why RFC 4402 Was Replaced
sections.content:
RFC 7802 obsoletes RFC 4402 and reclassifies it as Historic. RFC 4402 started the PRF+ counter at 1, but a number of implementations start it at 0. The original specification would therefore not interoperate with those implementations.

This RFC writes down the version that matches them: its formula runs from T0 upward, so the first counter value is 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups were counting from different numbers, so their answers never matched. This fixes the count so everyone agrees.

sections.title: The PRF+ Construction
sections.content:
The output of the GSS-API PRF is a PRF+ function based on the Kerberos V pseudo-random function (from RFC 3961) for the encryption type of the context's keys. It is keyed with the key chosen by the prf_key input parameter of GSS_Pseudo_random().

Each block is Tn = pseudo-random(K, n || S), where || is concatenation and n is a 32-bit unsigned number in network byte order. The blocks are concatenated and truncated to the requested length L.

Because the counter is 32 bits, the maximum output is 2^32 times the output size of the pseudo-random function for the key's encryption type.
sections.plainLanguage: Take the secret, mix it with 0, then 1, then 2 and so on. Each mix gives a chunk, and you glue chunks together until you have enough.

sections.title: Choosing the Key
sections.content:
The PRF+ MUST be keyed according to the prf_key parameter. For GSS_C_PRF_KEY_FULL, use the sub-session key asserted by the acceptor if there is one, otherwise the one asserted by the initiator if there is one, otherwise the ticket's session key.

For GSS_C_PRF_KEY_PARTIAL, use the sub-session key asserted by the initiator if there is one, otherwise the ticket's session key.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a pecking order of which secret to use. The newest, most special one wins, and the ordinary ticket secret is the last resort.

sections.title: Input Limits
sections.content:
RFC 4401 limits the input to 2^14 octets. If the input is longer than that and exceeds the implementation's resources, the mechanism MUST return GSS_S_FAILURE with GSS_KRB5_S_KG_INPUT_TOO_LONG as the minor status code.

There are no IANA actions now. If a registry of GSS-API symbols and constants is created, that minor status code should be added to it.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone hands over too much to stir in, the program says no and gives a specific reason.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The PRFs of Kerberos V encryption types use a key derived from the context's session keys and should preserve the forward security properties of the mechanisms' key exchanges. Legacy encryption types may be weak, particularly the single-DES types.

Using ticket session keys when initiators and acceptors fail to assert sub-session keys is dangerous, because ticket reuse can lead to key reuse. So initiators should always assert sub-session keys, and acceptors should assert them at least when initiators fail to do so.

The cost of the PRF+ varies with the encryption type and generally grows with input and output length. The counter allows the work to be parallelized.
sections.plainLanguage: Reusing the same ticket secret is risky, so each side should bring a fresh one. Old, weak locks stay weak no matter what.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Appendix A gives test vectors from the MIT implementation, provided by Greg Hudson. Each encryption type has two cases: an empty input and a 61-byte input, both with 44 bytes of output. The 61-byte input is just enough to produce a partial second MD5 or SHA1 hash block with the four-byte counter prefix, and 44 bytes of output needs two full and one partial PRF output for all existing encryption types.

The types covered are des-cbc-crc, des3-cbc-sha1, rc4-hmac, aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96, aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96, camellia128-cts-cmac and camellia256-cts-cmac. All keys were randomly generated.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer key lets anyone check their work and see that their program gets the same results as everyone else's.

data.title: PRF+
data.code:
PRF+(K, L, S) = truncate(L, T0 || T1 || .. || Tn)

Tn = pseudo-random(K, n || S)
